journeyIntro: For colleagues, managers and teammates. Practise clear requests, feedback and respectful collaboration.

lessons.title: Make Clear Requests
lessons.summary: Say what you need without guessing games.

steps.title: Vague asks get vague results
steps.body: “Can you send that over at some point?” leaves everyone guessing. A clear request says what you need, by when and, ideally, why it matters.

steps.prompt: You need a teammate’s sales figures to finish a report, and they haven’t arrived. What do you send?

options.text: “You’re holding the whole report up.”
options.why: Blame puts them on the back foot and doesn’t tell them what you actually need or when.

options.text: Say nothing and hope they remember.
options.why: They may not know it’s urgent, and you’ll be left scrambling at the deadline.

options.text: “Could you send the Q3 figures by Thursday noon? I need them for Friday’s report.”
options.why: It names the exact thing, the deadline and the reason, so it’s easy to prioritise.

steps.prompt: Add the deadline.
steps.after: so I can finish the report?
steps.why: A specific time removes the guesswork and makes the request easy to plan around.

steps.prompt: What makes asking colleagues for things hard for you?
options: Feeling I should do it all
steps.reply: Common at work. A clear, polite request is a kindness: it saves everyone time.

steps.prompt: Clear request or vague one?

cards.text: “Could you send the Q3 numbers by 3pm today?”
“Sam, could you review slides 4–6 by Friday?”

steps.why: Clear requests name who, what and when, so people can say yes and actually deliver.

steps.body: Make one work request today that says exactly what you need, by when and why.

steps.title: Waiting to talk isn’t listening
steps.body: In meetings it’s easy to spend someone’s whole point preparing your reply. Then you answer what you expected them to say, not what they said.

steps.prompt: In a planning meeting, a colleague raises concerns about your launch plan. What’s the most useful response?

options.text: Cut in to defend the plan before they finish.
options.why: Interrupting can make you look defensive and you may miss a concern that’s genuinely useful.

options.text: Check your phone until they’re done.
options.why: Others notice, and the colleague may feel their input doesn’t matter to you.

options.text: “So your main worry is that two weeks isn’t enough for testing?”
options.why: Summarising checks you’ve understood and shows you take their concern seriously.

steps.title: Summarise, then respond
steps.body: A quick summary like “So you’re saying…” takes seconds. It catches misunderstandings early and often calms a tense meeting.

steps.prompt: Check you understood.
steps.why: It reflects their point fairly without shrinking or exaggerating it.

steps.prompt: When do you find it hardest to listen at work?
steps.reply: Knowing that moment helps. Try a quick summary there before you respond.

steps.title: A worried message

lines.text: Honestly, I’m not sure the new booking process is going to work.

steps.prompt: You designed the process. Reply:

options.text: It’s only been a week, give it time.
options.why: Dismissing it means you lose useful feedback, and she may stop raising issues.

options.text: It worked fine in testing.
options.why: Defending the work closes the door before you’ve heard what’s going wrong.

options.text: Thanks for flagging. What are clients getting stuck on?
options.reaction: Mostly step two. I’ll send you some examples!
options.why: Thanking her and asking for specifics turns a worry into something you can fix together.

steps.body: In your next meeting, summarise one colleague’s point in a sentence before giving your own view.

lessons.title: Build Small Connections
lessons.summary: Warmth can fit into a busy workday.

steps.title: Warmth makes work work
steps.body: Teams that feel connected tend to share problems sooner and help each other more. It doesn’t take team-building days, just small, regular warmth.

steps.prompt: A new person joins your project team this week. What’s the most helpful thing you can do?

options.text: Leave it to their manager to sort out.
options.why: Managers help, but a friendly face from the team makes the first week much less lonely.

options.text: Say hello, and show them one thing that’ll make their week easier.
options.why: A warm welcome plus something practical helps them feel included and useful quickly.

options.text: Quiz them on what they know about the project.
options.why: It can feel like a test on day one, when they’re still finding their feet.

steps.prompt: Offer something useful.
steps.why: Practical help in the first days is remembered for a long time.

steps.prompt: How do you usually connect with colleagues?
steps.reply: Any of those can work. One small extra moment of warmth a week goes a long way.

steps.prompt: Match each moment with a small way to connect.
steps.why: Small, timely gestures make work feel friendlier and build the trust teams rely on when things get hard.

steps.body: Offer one colleague a small, practical kindness today: an introduction, a tip or a quick hello.

steps.title: Available isn’t the same as helpful
steps.body: Answering every message instantly can feel helpful, but constant interruptions make it hard to do your best work, for anyone.

steps.prompt: A colleague keeps calling during your morning focus block, and your own deadline is slipping. What do you do?

options.text: “I’m heads-down until two. Can I call you straight after?”
options.why: It protects your focus, gives a clear time and shows you’re still there for them.

options.text: Keep answering every call and miss your deadline.
options.why: You’ll end up behind and stressed, and they never learn when to reach you.

options.text: Ignore their calls all week.
options.why: Silence can look unhelpful and may cause bigger problems if something is urgent.

steps.title: Make your hours visible
steps.body: Block focus time in your calendar, set a status and say when you’ll be available. Clear signals mean fewer interruptions and fewer hard feelings.

steps.prompt: Offer a time instead.
steps.why: A clear alternative keeps the boundary friendly and the collaboration intact.

steps.prompt: Protecting your focus time. Put these in order.
items: Tell the team when it is
steps.why: Making the boundary visible before you need it means people can respect it without feeling shut out.

steps.body: Block one focus window in your calendar this week and let your team know when you’ll be reachable.

lessons.title: Be Dependable
lessons.summary: Clear updates matter as much as delivery.

steps.title: Bad news early is good news
steps.body: Everyone misses deadlines sometimes. What damages trust is the surprise. Flag problems early and people can plan around them.

steps.prompt: You realise your part of the project will miss Friday’s deadline. It’s Tuesday. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and see if anyone asks about it.
options.why: By Friday there’s no time left to adjust, and the surprise hurts more than the delay.

options.text: Say it’s nearly done and work late to catch up.
options.why: If it slips anyway, people will doubt your updates in future.

options.text: Tell the team now, explain the impact and suggest a new date.
options.why: An early, honest update with a plan lets others adjust and shows you’re reliable.

steps.prompt: Give an honest update.
steps.after: . I can deliver it on Tuesday.
steps.why: Plain facts plus a new date are the most useful update you can give a team.

steps.prompt: Why is flagging delays hard for you?
steps.reply: Understandable. Early updates usually earn more trust than quietly catching up.

steps.title: One more thing

lines.text: Quick one: could you also take on the client deck this week?

steps.prompt: Your week is already full. Reply:

options.text: Happy to help. To do it well, which should I move: the audit or the training plan?
options.reaction: Good shout, push the training plan to next week.
options.why: You stay helpful and honest about capacity, so you can deliver what you take on.

options.text: Sure, no problem!
options.why: An easy yes now can mean missed deadlines later, which hurts trust more.

options.text: I can’t, I’m swamped.
options.reaction: Oh. Okay, I’ll find someone else.
options.why: Honest, but a flat no misses the chance to work out priorities together.

steps.body: Send one honest progress update this week before anyone asks for it.

steps.title: Challenge the plan, not the person
steps.body: Good teams disagree about ideas often, and respectfully. Framing a concern as a question about the work keeps it from feeling personal.

steps.prompt: A teammate proposes a timeline you think is risky. What’s the best way to raise it?

options.text: “What are we assuming about testing time? It feels tight to me.”
options.why: A question about assumptions invites the team to look at the risk together.

options.text: “That timeline’s ridiculous.”
options.why: It attacks the idea’s owner, so the conversation turns defensive instead of useful.

options.text: Agree in the meeting, then complain afterwards.
options.why: The risk goes unaddressed, and complaining privately can erode team trust.

steps.title: When it’s more than disagreement
steps.body: Disagreeing about work is healthy. Bullying, harassment or feeling unsafe is not. Talk to someone you trust, HR or a support service if it happens.

steps.prompt: Frame it as a question.
steps.why: Asking about assumptions focuses on the plan and invites everyone to check it.

steps.prompt: Is there a concern at work you’ve held back? How could you raise it as a question?
About the idea, or about the person?

cards.text: “I’m worried the timeline leaves no buffer.”
“What if testing takes longer than planned?”
“Could we compare it with a six-week plan?”

steps.why: Keeping a disagreement on the idea lets you push back hard without damaging the working relationship.

steps.body: Raise one work concern as a question about the plan, rather than a judgement of the person.

lessons.title: Give Useful Feedback
lessons.summary: Be specific and kind when something slips.

steps.title: Specific beats general
steps.body: “Be more careful” leaves people unsure what to change. Useful feedback names what happened, why it matters and what would help next time.

steps.prompt: A colleague’s handover notes missed two client deadlines, and you nearly got caught out. What helps most?

options.text: Mention in the team chat that some people are careless.
options.why: Public, vague criticism embarrasses them without saying what to change.

options.text: Tell them which details were missing and suggest a short handover checklist.
options.why: It’s specific about the gap and offers a practical fix, so it’s easy to act on.

options.text: Quietly redo every handover yourself from now on.
options.why: You take on extra work, and they never get the chance to improve.

steps.title: Keep it private and kind
steps.body: Give feedback one to one, soon after it happens, and assume good intent. “I know you were rushed. Could we add deadlines to handovers?”

steps.prompt: Name the specific gap.
steps.before: The handover was helpful, but it
steps.why: Naming exactly what was missing gives them something concrete to fix.

steps.prompt: Giving useful feedback. Put these in order.
steps.why: Facts and impact keep it fair and specific, and agreeing next steps turns criticism into a plan.

steps.body: Give one colleague a piece of specific, kindly worded feedback, with a practical suggestion.

steps.title: The sting is normal
steps.body: Even fair feedback can sting, and the urge to defend yourself is natural. Pausing to get curious turns criticism into something you can use.

steps.prompt: Your manager says your weekly updates are “too brief”. What’s the best response?

options.text: Explain why each past update was fine.
options.why: Defending every point can look like you’re not listening, and you miss what they want.

options.text: “Thanks. Which details would make them more useful to you?”
options.why: A curious question gets you specifics, and shows you take the feedback seriously.

options.text: Decide your manager just doesn’t like you.
options.why: Jumping to that story can colour every future conversation with them.

steps.prompt: Ask for specifics.
steps.why: An example turns vague feedback into something you can act on straight away.

steps.prompt: When you get critical feedback, what’s your first reaction?
steps.reply: Your first reaction is fine. What helps is the curious question you ask next.

steps.prompt: Match each defensive reply with a better one.
steps.why: Curious replies keep feedback coming and help you improve, while defensive ones make people stop telling you.

steps.body: The next time you get feedback, thank them and ask one clarifying question before responding.

steps.title: Quick repairs keep teams safe
steps.body: Small slips at work, like interrupting or a sharp email, can make colleagues hold back. A quick, simple repair keeps the team feeling safe to speak.

steps.prompt: During a team presentation, you talked over a teammate twice. You noticed them go quiet. What now?

options.text: Suggest they speak up more next time.
options.why: It puts the problem on them, when the interrupting came from you.

options.text: “I interrupted you earlier, sorry. Please finish your point.”
options.why: Owning it in the moment and handing the floor back repairs things quickly.

options.text: Avoid them for the rest of the week.
options.why: Avoidance lets awkwardness grow and can quietly harm how you work together.

steps.prompt: Hand the floor back.
steps.why: Giving the floor back shows respect and makes the apology real.

steps.prompt: Which small work slip do you find hardest to own?
steps.reply: Good to know. A quick, simple repair there will build a lot of goodwill.

steps.title: A short reply

lines.text: I think we should go with option B for the client.
Fine. Whatever you think is best.

steps.prompt: Leo had argued for option A. Reply:

options.text: Great, B it is then 👍
options.why: Taking “fine” at face value can leave a teammate quietly frustrated and disengaged.

options.text: That sounded like a not-so-fine “fine” 🙂 Can we chat about A? I want to get it right.
options.reaction: Ha, yeah. Thanks. I’ve got a couple of points on A.
options.why: You noticed the tension and invited them back in, which repairs it before it grows.

options.text: No need for the attitude.
options.why: Calling it out sharply makes them defensive and deepens the tension.

steps.body: After your next tense moment at work, make a brief repair within the same day.

steps.title: Everyone’s job is no one’s job
steps.body: When ownership is fuzzy, tasks fall through the gaps and people quietly blame each other. Clear owners and deadlines protect both work and trust.

steps.prompt: You and a teammate each assumed the other would follow up with an important client. It’s been a week. What helps?

options.text: Agree who owns it, by when, and how you’ll confirm it’s done.
options.why: Clear ownership fixes this follow-up and stops the same gap happening again.

options.text: Assume someone will sort it eventually.
options.why: That’s how it slipped in the first place; the client may notice before anyone acts.

options.text: Post a vague “Can someone handle this?” in the team chat.
options.why: Group messages without an owner often get likes but no action.

steps.title: Who, what, by when
steps.body: End meetings by naming who does what, by when. It feels formal at first, but it saves so many awkward “I thought you were doing it” chats.

steps.prompt: Which shared task at work needs a clearer owner?
steps.placeholder: The task is… and the owner should be…

steps.prompt: Clear ownership, or an assumption?

cards.text: Ending meetings by naming who does what
A shared list with names and dates

steps.why: Naming who owns each task is how teams avoid the gaps where everyone assumed someone else had it.

steps.body: Clarify the owner, next step and deadline for one shared task this week.
